title: SIMD & Vector Processing
summary: One instruction operating on many data elements at once — the ISA extensions behind it, and the code shapes that actually benefit.

slides.markdown:
**SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data)** lets one instruction apply the same operation to several data elements at once — add 4 pairs of integers in one instruction instead of 4 separate scalar adds. It's data parallelism, orthogonal to the instruction- and thread-level parallelism covered elsewhere ([ilp-fundamentals](ilp-fundamentals)).

SIMD is why one core processes large uniform arrays (images, audio, matrix rows) far faster than its scalar instruction count suggests — parallelism is packed into each instruction's data width, not spread across cores.

SIMD needs somewhere to hold multiple packed values at once: **vector registers** are wide registers (128, 256, even 512 bits) that hold several scalar values side by side — a 128-bit register might hold four 32-bit integers, treated as one unit by a SIMD instruction.

A single SIMD add on a 128-bit register performs four independent 32-bit additions in the time a scalar core would need four separate instructions — the register width, not extra instructions, is what supplies the parallelism.

slides.sectionTitle: One SIMD add vs four scalar adds
slides.markdown:
![A SIMD add operating on 4 packed integers in one instruction, compared to 4 separate scalar add instructions](assets/simd-vs-scalar.svg)

Both compute the same four sums, but SIMD issues, decodes, and executes as **one** instruction across all four lanes, while scalar pays the full instruction cost four times — the gain compounds as vector width grows (8, 16 elements on wider extensions).

assets.alt: A SIMD add operating on 4 packed integers in one instruction, compared to 4 separate scalar add instructions

slides.markdown:
Every mainstream ISA added SIMD extensions once data-parallel workloads (multimedia, then ML) became common: **SSE and AVX** on x86 progressively widened vector registers from 128 to 256 to 512 bits, and **NEON** on ARM provides 128-bit SIMD for mobile/embedded cores.

These aren't niche instructions — compilers auto-vectorize ordinary loops into them by default at reasonable optimization levels, and most "fast" numeric code on a CPU today is fast largely *because* it's using these extensions, whether or not the programmer wrote any SIMD-specific code themselves.

A compiler auto-vectorizes a simple loop without any special syntax:

```c
// scalar source
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}
```

```asm
; compiler-generated (conceptual, AVX-style)
vmovups ymm0, [a + i]   ; load 8 floats from a
vmovups ymm1, [b + i]   ; load 8 floats from b
vaddps  ymm2, ymm0, ymm1 ; add all 8 pairs at once
vmovups [c + i], ymm2   ; store 8 results
```

The scalar loop's body never changes — the compiler recognizes the iterations are independent and rewrites the object code to process 8 elements per iteration instead of 1, with no `#pragma` or intrinsic required at this optimization level.

slides.sectionTitle: SIMD vs scalar, and SIMD vs SIMT
slides.markdown:
| | Scalar loop | SIMD |
|---|---|---|
| Elements/instruction | 1 | 4/8/16 (register-width dependent) |
| Requirement | None | Uniform control flow, aligned/contiguous data ideally |
| Throughput on uniform data | Baseline | Multiples of baseline |

SIMD is also easy to confuse with **SIMT** ([simt-execution-model](simt-execution-model), GPUs) — SIMD is one thread operating on a wide vector register; SIMT is many separate threads executing the same instruction in lockstep across separate ALU lanes. Related idea, different mechanism.

**How to decide:** SIMD pays off on data-parallel loops with predictable, uniform access; it earns little on branchy, irregular code.

SIMD assumes every lane runs the **same operation** in lockstep — a loop branching differently per element (`if (a[i]>0) c[i]=f(a[i]); else c[i]=g(a[i]);`) can't cleanly map to one instruction, since lanes would need different code paths.

Compilers can use **masking** (compute both branches, select per lane) at the cost of wasted work, but heavy data-dependent branching often defeats vectorization entirely, falling back to scalar code — a common, easily-missed reason a "should be fast" loop stays slow.
